preserved_objections.basis: The claimed "distributed occlusion force" mechanism directly contradicts the fundamental operating principle of peristaltic pumps, which relies on sequential occlusion of tubing lines to create directional flow. The proposed simultaneous occlusion would prevent fluid movement entirely, as described in [doi:10.1016/s0262-1762(03)00715-6] which explains that peristaltic action requires sequential compression.

The 120×80×50mm envelope boundary condition cannot accommodate a multi-point rotor contact geometry capable of applying distributed force to multiple 2.5mm bore tubing lines simultaneously while maintaining the required 0.5 mL/min flow rate. The mathematically required contact points would necessitate a rotor diameter exceeding the device height constraint, violating the boundary condition.

The candidate's own evidence bundle contradicts the proposed solution. [doi:10.32786/2071-9485-2018-03-324-329] explicitly states that "optimal peristaltic pump performance requires precisely controlled sequential occlusion" rather than simultaneous force distribution, directly refuting the core mechanism of the proposed invention.

The claimed effect of "maintaining 0.5 mL/min flow with <2% dosing accuracy" is impossible if all tubing lines are occluded simultaneously, as this would completely block flow. The baseline performance requires sequential occlusion to create the peristaltic effect, which the proposed design eliminates entirely.

The "multi-point rotor contact geometry with equal force distribution" cannot be implemented with 3D printing technology at the required precision. The [doi:10.1016/s0262-1762(04)00163-4] reference on compact pumps specifies that rotor contact points must be manufactured to within ±0.05mm tolerance to maintain dosing accuracy, which exceeds the capabilities of standard 3D printing processes.

The testable prediction of "force distribution uniformity across tubing lines measured via pressure sensors will show <5% variation" fails to account for the dynamic nature of peristaltic action. Pressure sensors cannot measure static force distribution in a system that requires dynamic sequential occlusion to function, as explained in [doi:10.52338/jows.2026.5561] which details the physical effects of peristaltic pumps.
